paras: The lynching of John Wood was the reported killing of a Black man at Denison, Texas, on March 28, 1888. Wood was accused of abducting Amelia Wilson, described as a white girl, and was said to have been lynched for it. The case reached readers only as a one-sentence wire item and as a line in a year-end roll of lynching victims.

According to the wire item, John Wood, called "a Texas negro," was lynched "on the 28th" at Denison "for abducting Amelia Wilson, a white girl." The item placed the date in March, since it ran in early April beside other news dated the 28th to the 30th of the previous month. It did not describe the abduction charge, the people who killed Wood, how he was killed, or whether he had been in custody.

No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage. At the end of the year, a list headed "Victims of Judge Lynch" entered the case under March as "28—John Wood at Denison, Texas."

The story circulated in a syndicated "Domestic" news digest printed by small weeklies in Minnesota and Dakota Territory, first in the Mower County Transcript on April 4, 1888. The Kanabec County Times, the Big Stone City Herald, the Griggs Courier and The Progress of White Earth, Minnesota, ran the same sentence word for word between April 5 and April 14. In each copy the lynching sat without a headline between a report of heavy rain in Georgia and Alabama and a fire at Aurora, Illinois, and the abduction was given as the cause without qualification.

The year-end list ran on December 26 in the Union County Courier of Elk Point, Dakota, and The True Northerner of Paw Paw, Michigan, giving only Wood's name, the place and the day. No account from a Texas paper, and no Black newspaper's report, appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Lynching of John Wood
bases: The wire item says Wood was 'lynched' for an alleged abduction, and a year-end list counts him among the 'Victims of Judge Lynch' (A1, A6).

Wood was reported 'lynched' for an alleged abduction of a white girl and listed among the year's 'Victims of Judge Lynch', which implies an extralegal killing under a pretext of punishment (A1, A6); no report describes the mob, its size or the method, so the group element rests on the word 'lynched' alone.
Every April report is the same one-sentence wire item (A1-A5), and the year-end list (A6, A7) adds only the name, place and day, so no independent account corroborates the details.
